cues.en: I'm delighted to formally introduce Steve Blank, who is currently a lecturer at Berkeley's Haas School of Business. Steve is a serial entrepreneur, having spent nearly 30 years as a founder and executive of high-tech companies here in Silicon Valley. His most recent venture was co-founding the enterprise software company firm, E. Epiphany.
cues.zh: 我很荣幸正式介绍 Steve Blank，他目前是伯克利哈斯商学院的讲师。Steve 是一位连续创业者，在硅谷的高科技公司做了近 30 年的创始人和高管。他最近一次创业是联合创办了企业软件公司 E.piphany。

cues.en: In total, Steve has been involved or has co-founded eight Silicon Valley startups ranging from semiconductors to video games and personal computers to supercomputers. He's a strong communicator and has combined that with fervent research where he spends a great deal of time in the academic community, recently teaching entrepreneurship at Stanford's Graduate School of Engineering and is currently teaching in the joint Berkeley Columbia Executive MBA program.
cues.zh: Steve 总共参与或联合创办过八家硅谷初创公司，领域涵盖半导体、视频游戏、个人电脑到超级计算机。他非常善于表达，并且热衷于研究，在学术界投入了大量时间，最近在斯坦福工程学院教授创业课程，目前则在伯克利与哥伦比亚大学合办的高管 MBA 项目任教。

cues.en: Steve sits on the IMVU board of directors, as well as the ever creative cafe press board. Please prepare yourself to be informed, entertained, and inspired, as Steve presents the secret history of Silicon Valley. It's my pleasure to welcome Steve to the stage. Thank you. Thank you. After that intro, I'm not sure I could live up to it, but I'll try. And I'll try to keep you from going to sleep as you eat your lunch.
cues.zh: Steve 是 IMVU 董事会成员，同时也是创意十足的 CafePress 的董事会成员。请大家做好准备，在接下来的演讲中，Steve 将为你带来资讯、乐趣与启发——硅谷的秘密历史。欢迎 Steve 上台。谢谢。谢谢。听完这个介绍，我都不知道自己能不能配得上了，但我会尽力。我也会尽力让大家在吃午饭的时候不打瞌睡。

cues.en: I thought it'd be worth maybe just starting of how I even got interested in this subject, the history of Silicon Valley. As was noted, I teach entrepreneurship to a bunch of eager next-generation entrepreneurs at both Stanford and Berkeley. And I was at Stanford, and I decided to ask, does anybody know how Silicon Valley got started? And I would have expected an erudite and deep conversation. And what I got is,
cues.zh: 我想不妨先从我是怎么对硅谷历史这个主题产生兴趣的说起。刚才提到过，我在斯坦福和伯克利给一群热切的下一代创业者教创业课。有一次在斯坦福，我决定问问：有谁知道硅谷是怎么起步的吗？我本来期待一场有深度、有见地的讨论，结果我得到的是——

cues.en: Oh, we know who started Silicon Valley. It started with the internet. What? Oh, yeah, yeah. There was this old guy. His name was, I don't know, Mark Andreessen. And I went, old guy, Mark Andreessen. OK. And I said, well, you guys are engineering. So can you think a little harder? What do you use besides the net? Oh, we get it. OK, personal computers. That were the old days. And there's some real old guy. I think he's a grandfather named Steve Jobs.
cues.zh: "哦，我们知道硅谷是谁开创的。是从互联网开始的。" 什么？"对啊对啊，有一个老家伙，他叫……我忘了，好像是 Marc Andreessen。" 我心想，老家伙？Marc Andreessen？好吧。我说，你们可是学工程的，能不能再想想？除了互联网，你们还用什么？"哦，懂了，个人电脑。" 那是很久以前的事了。还有一个真正的老家伙，我记得他叫 Steve Jobs，好像都当爷爷了。

cues.en: Ooh, feeling very old, very old. I said, no, no, no, what makes up computers and where they come from? Oh, we get it, integrated circuits. And I think they found buried tablets with these guys named Moore and Noyce. And I realized that we were going to have some education to do. And in reality, this talk is about the genesis of Silicon Valley in the 1940s and 50s.
cues.zh: 唉，我感觉自己瞬间老了很多。我说，不对不对，电脑是由什么构成的？它们从哪儿来？"哦，懂了，集成电路。" 我估计他们还挖出了刻着 Moore 和 Noyce 这两位名字的石板。我意识到我们得给他们补补课了。其实，这次演讲讲的就是硅谷在二十世纪四五十年代的起源。

cues.en: Even as Hewlett-Packard, one of our earliest companies, were getting started, is about Silicon Valley and the defense business. Now, I should point out that this conversation with my students is occurring in the Terman Engineering Building. And I'm only getting laughter from half of you, because that's the half that actually knows computer history, and I will get laughter from the rest of you by the time the talk is over.
cues.zh: 甚至在惠普——我们最早的公司之一——起步的时候，硅谷就已经与国防产业密不可分了。需要指出的是，刚才我和学生的那番对话，就发生在 Terman 工程大楼里。在座的只有一半人在笑，因为那才是一半真正懂计算机历史的人，等演讲结束时，我会让剩下的人也笑起来。

cues.en: So the focus today is a part of computer history you might not be aware of, and it starts all the way back in World War II. But first, a couple of caveats about this talk. Giving a history talk in the Computer History Museum just kind of makes me insist on putting up these three caveats. I'm not a professional historian, therefore I could get away with saying anything today.
cues.zh: 所以今天的主题，是一段你可能不太了解的计算机历史，它要一直追溯到二战时期。不过开讲前，我想先做几点声明。在计算机历史博物馆做历史讲座，让我不得不先打这三点“预防针”。我不是专业的历史学家，所以今天就算信口开河大家也别介意。

cues.en: Two is some or all of this is probably wrong because I'm a marketeer by training. And then third, for those of you who come from the black world, all secrets are from open source literature and I've been saving every reference in case they decide to come and ask me where I got this from. So I'm going to tell this story in six short vignettes. The first one,
cues.zh: 第二，其中一部分甚至全部内容可能都是错的，因为我是做市场营销出身的。第三，对于那些来自秘密情报领域的朋友，这里所有的“秘密”都来自公开文献，而且我都保留了出处，免得有人找上门来问我是从哪儿搞到的。接下来我将通过六个小故事来展开。第一个故事，

cues.en: Not so short, maybe about 20 minutes, and it might make you wonder what the heck does it have to do with Silicon Valley, but trust me, by the end, it'll make sense. And the first story is World War II, the first electronic war. By itself, for some of you, this should be a surprise, because every World War II movie you have ever seen that included airplanes on bombing missions is wrong. Every one of them.
cues.zh: 其实也不算短，大概要讲20分钟，可能会让你纳闷：这跟硅谷到底有什么关系？但相信我，听到最后你就会恍然大悟。第一个故事是关于二战——也就是历史上第一次电子战。单是这一点，可能就足以让一些人惊讶，因为你们看过的所有包含轰炸机作战情节的二战电影，其实全都是错的。每一部都错了。

cues.en: Not because anybody is lying to you, but because the people who made the movies and wrote the books don't know about what I'm about to tell you. For those of you who know your World War II history, Germany and Russia, Soviet Union at the time, attacked Poland in September 1939 and World War II breaks out. By 1940, the Germans have overrun continental Europe. Britain stands by itself.
cues.zh: 倒不是有人故意骗你，而是拍电影和写书的人根本不知道我接下来要讲的事情。熟悉二战历史的人都知道，1939年9月，德国和当时的苏联进攻波兰，二战爆发。到了1940年，德军横扫欧洲大陆，英国陷入孤立无援的境地。

cues.en: In June 1941, the Germans turned on their Soviet allies and launched the invasion of the Soviet Union. By December 1941, the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, and Germany declares war on the United States. And we're now at war with the Germans and the Japanese. And while the Soviets are fighting the Germans on land, the only way the Allies
cues.zh: 1941年6月，德国倒戈相向，对其盟友苏联发动入侵。到了1941年12月，日本偷袭珍珠港，德国随即对美国宣战。至此，我们开始同时与德日两国交战。当苏联人在陆地上与德军浴血奋战时，盟军唯一

cues.en: can affect German strategic war fighting capability is by mounting a strategic bombing campaign from the largest aircraft carrier in the world, Great Britain. And from 1942, 1943, until June 6, 1944, the only way the British and Americans can help the Soviets who are fighting massive land battles in the East.
cues.zh: 能打击德国战略作战能力的手段，就是以全球最大的“航空母舰”——大不列颠岛为跳板，展开战略轰炸行动。从1942年、1943年，一直到1944年6月6日，英美两国要想支援在东线进行大规模陆战的苏联，唯一的办法

cues.en: is to start to try to destroy the German capability to wage war. And they did that by targeting critical infrastructure of the German war machine. They said we were going to bomb petroleum infrastructure, aircraft manufacturing infrastructure, chemical infrastructure, transportation infrastructure. And the targeting committees decided they were going to take these out a piece at a time. The Americans and British split up.
cues.zh: 就是想方设法摧毁德国的战争潜能。他们采取的做法是打击纳粹战争机器的关键基础设施。他们计划轰炸石油设施、飞机制造厂、化工设施以及交通基础设施。目标选定委员会决定逐步摧毁这些目标。随后美英两国进行了分工。

cues.en: the air campaign. The British bombed at night. They had a strategy called area bombing, which was euphemistically described as de-housing the population. And if you were in one of those houses, it was kind of unfortunate. The British used Lancasters and Halifax bombers. They flew from anywhere from 7,000 to 17,000 feet, unpressurized airplanes. The Americans, being Americans, said, hey.
cues.zh: 空中战役。英国人在夜间轰炸。他们有个战略叫“区域轰炸”，委婉说法是“清除人口住房”。如果你就在那些房子里，那确实挺倒霉。英国人用兰开斯特和哈利法克斯轰炸机。飞行高度从7000到17000英尺不等，都是非增压飞机。美国人嘛，毕竟是美国人，说：嘿。

cues.en: We could hit anything. What's this about area bombing? And you guys are at night? We're going to fly during the day. And not only are we going to fly during the day, we're going to put bombs right through the chimney of our targets. Because we have the world's best pilots and planes and strategic bombing. That's us. And we flew B-17s and B-24s, also flying 15,000 to 25,000 feet unpressurized. Trip from England to Germany.
cues.zh: 我们能命中任何目标。区域轰炸是怎么回事？你们还夜间出动？我们要白天飞。不光白天飞，我们还要把炸弹从目标的烟囱里扔进去。因为我们有世界上最好的飞行员、飞机和战略轰炸。说的就是我们。我们飞B-17和B-24，同样在15000到25000英尺的非增压环境下飞行。从英国到德国的航程。

cues.en: and back. These planes took off from England, formed up over the United Kingdom, and flew in formation. In fact, did you turn up the audio? The British in the American air war in Europe had 28,000 active combat planes. Just to give you some scale, there were 40,000 planes lost or damaged. Almost half American, half British. The entire jet fleet today worldwide, by the way, 20,000 planes.
cues.zh: 再飞回来。这些飞机从英格兰起飞，在英国上空完成编队，然后编队飞行。其实，你把音频调大了吗？在欧洲对德空中战争中，英美一方有28000架现役作战飞机。给你们一个规模参照：共有40000架飞机损失或受损，几乎一半美国、一半英国。顺便说，今天全世界整个喷气机队也就2万架。

cues.en: And we lost just in the Allied air war on the Western Front 160,000 airmen lost in the air, not just captured, killed. Their average age was about 20. And when these planes formed up, it looked something like this. They took off from their bases one at a time and orbited as they climbed in altitude for all heading towards German. And they believed, at least over England and as they crossed the channel, they were safe.
cues.zh: 仅西线盟军空战中，我们就损失了16万名空勤人员，他们是在空中丧生，不只是被俘，而是阵亡。平均年龄大约20岁。这些飞机编队时，看起来大致像这样。它们从各自基地一架架起飞，在爬升时盘旋，全都飞向德国。而且他们相信，至少在英格兰上空、在穿越英吉利海峡时，自己是安全的。

cues.en: But they were wrong. What they never knew is even over England, they were being detected by the German air defense system, the Camulerine. The Germans had built an integrated electronic air defense network. It covered France, the low countries, all the way into Germany. And its function was to do three things, warn and detect, target and aim the German weapons.
cues.zh: 但他们错了。他们从不知道的是，即使在英格兰上空，他们也已被德国防空系统Camulerine探测到。德国人建了一套综合电子防空网络，覆盖法国、低地国家，一直延伸到德国。它的功能是三件事：预警探测、瞄准引导德军武器。

cues.en: and destroy their American and British bombers before they got to the targets, or if they couldn't do that before they returned home. The Germans needed to make strategic bombing too painful for the Allies to continue. Just to give you a scale of this, here's a map of just the early warning radars in occupied France. The Germans had two types of early warning radars. The first one was called the mammoth 200 mile range.
cues.zh: 并在美英轰炸机抵达目标前摧毁它们；如果做不到，也要在它们返航回家前摧毁。德国人要让战略轰炸对盟军来说痛苦到无法继续。给你们一个规模参照，这是一张仅被占法国境内预警雷达的地图。德国有两种预警雷达。第一种叫Mammoth，探测距离200英里。

cues.en: 100 feet wide, it was the first phased array radar, and this is 1942. There were 20 of these. But the backbone of the German early warning system was something called the Wasserman. 150 mile range, 190 feet tall. 1942, there were 150 of these scattered across the periphery of Europe looking for these bomber streams.
cues.zh: 宽100英尺，这是第一部相控阵雷达，而这是1942年。这种雷达有20部。但德国预警系统的骨干是一种叫Wasserman的雷达。探测距离150英里，高190英尺。1942年，有150部这样的雷达散布在欧洲外围，搜寻这些轰炸机机群。

cues.en: Now, that was bad enough that the Germans knew the planes were coming, and they could see them all the way over England. But what happened when they crossed the channel was even more interesting. What the Allies encountered was a local air defense system, which was a box 30 by 20 miles. And inside each one of these boxes, called the Himmel Belt, was an integrated network of radars, NRA aircraft guns,
cues.zh: 这已经够糟了：德国人知道飞机要来了，甚至能在英格兰上空一路看到它们。但更耐人寻味的是它们飞越英吉利海峡后发生的事。盟军遇到的是一个局部防空系统，覆盖范围是一个 30 乘 20 英里的方框。每个这种方框叫 Himmel Belt，里面是一个综合网络，包括雷达、NRA 高射炮，

cues.en: fighters, and at nighttime searchlights. What a American or British bomber would see, if they could see the radar painting them, would be they'd first be detected by a local early warning radar called FREA. And then they'd be painted by another radar called the giant Würzburg. And the Würzburg was the first ground control intercept radar. It would fix the bomber in its sights.
cues.zh: 战斗机，以及夜间探照灯。一名美国或英国轰炸机飞行员——如果能看见雷达在照射自己——会经历的是：先被一部叫 FREA 的本地预警雷达发现。然后被另一部叫巨型 Würzburg 的雷达照射。Würzburg 是第一部地面控制拦截雷达。它会把轰炸机锁定在瞄准镜里。

cues.en: It would communicate with a fighter pilot, a German fighter pilot, and vector or talk him in to the direction of the bomber. And then amazingly, this is 1942, the German night fighters had their own onboard radar. And when they got within a couple of miles, they'd turn on their own radar, lock onto the bombers, find them, and shoot them down at night. The Freya, 90 mile range, steerable and mobile.
cues.zh: 它会与一名战斗机飞行员——一名德国战斗机飞行员——通信，并引导他，或用无线电把他引向轰炸机的方向。然后令人惊讶的是，这可是 1942 年，德国夜间战斗机已经自带机载雷达。当它们进入几英里范围内时，会打开自己的雷达，锁定轰炸机，找到它们，并在夜间把它们击落。Freya 雷达，90 英里探测距离，可转向且可机动。

cues.en: Mobile radar, early 1940s, 1,000 of these. The Würzburgs, the ones that were vectoring the German fighter pilots into the bomber stream, 45 miles, 25 feet wide, 1,500 of these deployed. And all this radar data, a map of the battle, where are the bombers, where are our fighters, what's the disposition of our forces, was going into something called the Himmel Belt.
cues.zh: 机动雷达，20 世纪 40 年代初，有 1,000 部。Würzburg 雷达——那些把德国战斗机飞行员引导进轰炸机流的——45 英里，25 英尺宽，部署了 1,500 部。所有这些雷达数据、一幅战场地图——轰炸机在哪里、我们的战斗机在哪里、我军部署如何——都汇总到一个叫 Himmel Belt 的系统里。

cues.en: Think of this as one of the first early air traffic control systems, but the goal was not to land your plane safely. So all the radars fed regional Himmel belts, operators worked in front of essentially a large movie screen, and the positions of the fighters, the bombers, and the targets were all displayed. And the fighters would orbit around the radio beacon, and the fighter controller would talk the fighter planes into the bomber stream.
cues.zh: 可以把它看作最早的一批空中交通管制系统之一，但目标不是让你的飞机安全降落。所有雷达都汇入地区性的 Himmel Belt，操作员在一大块电影银幕前工作，战斗机、轰炸机和目标的位置全都会显示出来。战斗机会绕着无线电信标盘旋，战斗机控制员则通过无线电把战斗机引进轰炸机流。

cues.en: They turn on their radar, acquire the target, and attack. Turn up the volume if we can. You might recognize this from 12 o'clock high. Notice they're all on oxygen. Turn up a bit more, please. See those little dots? Those aren't new clouds. Those black dots are actually anti-aircraft shells fired from guns on the ground. Now every World War II movie I've ever seen
cues.zh: 它们打开雷达，捕获目标，然后攻击。可以的话把音量调大。你可能在《Twelve O'Clock High》里见过这个。注意他们都戴着氧气面罩。请再调大一点。看到那些小点了吗？那不是新出现的云。那些黑点其实是地面火炮发射的高射炮弹。我看过的每一部二战电影里

cues.en: I showed you some flak. So as our bombers were being detected by early warning radar, then picked up in the Himmel belt, they'd have to fly through anti-aircraft fire and then a gauntlet of fighter planes. But what you really didn't know is those anti-aircraft guns, and there were a lot of them, 15,000 heavy flak guns on the Western Front, 400,000 German soldiers dedicated to doing nothing but trying to shoot planes out of the sky with guns.
cues.zh: 我都给你们看过一些高射炮火。所以，当我们的轰炸机被预警雷达发现，然后在 Himmel Belt 中被捕捉到，它们必须飞过高射炮火，再穿过战斗机组成的死亡通道。但你真正不知道的是，那些高射炮——而且数量很多，西线有 15,000 门重型高射炮，40 万德国士兵除了用火炮把飞机从天上打下来什么都不干。

cues.en: They were radar-directed, every one of them. They were fused for time. Luckily, the Germans hadn't perfected the proximity fuse, so these would be fused for time to explode at a certain altitude. But what the Germans had was a radar set next to every flak battery. And these were essentially fire control radars, 15-mile range, that directed the azimuth, elevation, and direction of the guns.
cues.zh: 它们全都是由雷达引导的，装的是定时引信。幸运的是，德国人当时还没完善近炸引信，所以这些炮弹采用定时引信，在特定高度爆炸。但德国人在每个防空炮阵地旁都配了一台雷达。这些本质上是火控雷达，探测范围15英里，用来引导火炮的方位角、仰角和朝向。

cues.en: 10 feet wide, and it made their anti-aircraft guns incredibly accurate. And not only were these steerable, they were mobile. New target threatened, put them under a truck, drag them to the next target. 5,000 of these were deployed across Germany. Now, the other thing that these bombers encountered were night fighters, if you were the British. Take a look at the front of these aircraft. From the beginning of 1942,
cues.zh: 天线有10英尺宽，让他们的防空炮精准得不可思议。而且这些雷达不仅能调转方向，还能移动。新目标受到威胁？直接挂在卡车后面，拖去下一个目标。德国全境部署了5000台这种雷达。另外，如果是英国轰炸机，还会遭遇夜间战斗机。看看这些飞机的机头。从1942年初开始，

cues.en: All German night fighters had their own onboard radar, two and a half mile range. They were directed to the bomber stream by ground radar. They turned on their radar, and in pitch black at night, they could find the bombers and try to shoot them down. Get the sound again? In the daytime, you didn't need radar in the fighters. You could see the bomber stream. A little louder, please.
cues.zh: 所有德国夜间战斗机都配有机载雷达，探测范围2.5英里。地面雷达会引导它们接近轰炸机群。接着它们开启机载雷达，在漆黑的夜晚找到轰炸机并试图击落。声音有了吗？在白天，战斗机不需要雷达，肉眼就能看到轰炸机群。麻烦声音再大一点。

cues.en: The bombers couldn't maneuver. They had to just keep going. And they were under constant attack, first by flak, then by fighters. And all they had for self-defense were machine guns, aimed by that little circle. That's it. Bombers, manual machine guns against fighters, flying for hours across occupied Europe to try to go over a target, drop some bombs.
cues.zh: 轰炸机无法机动，只能硬着头皮往前飞。而且它们不断受到攻击，先是防空炮，接着是战斗机。它们唯一的自卫武器就是机枪，全靠那个小圆圈准星来瞄准。仅此而已。轰炸机用手动机枪对抗战斗机，在沦陷的欧洲上空飞行数小时，只为飞到目标上空投下炸弹。

cues.en: So the German day fighters were also vectored by radar. While the day fighters could see the bomber streams when they're close, Germany and occupied Europe was a pretty big place. So to find the bomber stream, they also had to get directions. So the ground control intercept operators would talk the fighters into visual range, and you get these kinds of attacks. Now, sound again? Every World War II movie, of course, has the objective, which is to get over the target.
cues.zh: 所以德国的昼间战斗机也是由雷达引导的。虽然昼间战斗机在靠近时能肉眼看到机群，但德国和占领区面积很大。为了找到轰炸机群，他们也必须获取引导。地面截击引导员会通过无线电把战斗机引到视距范围内，于是就有了这种截击。声音又有了吗？当然，每部二战电影的核心目标都是飞抵目标上空。

cues.en: flown through the gauntlet of anti-aircraft fire, fighter planes. You're now over the target. And in fact, this film, you could see those black dots or flak flying through a flak stream. And you always, by the way, in a World War II movie hear this whistling. Now, I don't know if they had a microphone like on the bombs, but I think it's somebody in the back whistling. Now, the last scene you noticed was the perfectly clear day, and the bombs always hit the target.
cues.zh: 穿越了防空炮火和战斗机交织的重重火网，你终于到达了目标上空。实际上在这段胶片里，你能看到那些黑点就是防空炮火，飞机正在穿过弹幕。顺便提一句，在二战电影里总能听到这种尖啸声。我不知道他们是不是在炸弹上装了麦克风，但我猜多半是后台有人在吹口哨。刚才最后一幕大家注意到了，天气晴空万里，炸弹总是精准命中目标。

cues.en: Now, if anybody's been to Europe in the fall and winter, it's kind of cloudy. Not always, but it's kind of cloudy. And you know, I never even thought when I saw all these World War II movies, what did these guys do? Like fly once every three months? You know, it seemed like they were flying a lot. So how'd they see the target? Well, here's something else you never saw in a World War II movie. We had air-to-ground bombing radar.
cues.zh: 但去过秋冬季节欧洲的人都知道，那里经常多云。并非总是如此，但大多阴云密布。以前看那些二战电影时我就想：这些人平时到底怎么飞的？难道三个月才出动一次？但看起来他们飞得很频繁。那他们怎么看到目标的呢？这就涉及到二战电影里从没演过的东西了——我们有空对地轰炸雷达。

cues.en: We basically had radar aimed at the ground. Targets could be seen under clouds and rain. We could see outlines of major ground features, and we made map overlays of, yep, there's hamburger, here's the river, here's the coast, here's where it should be. Let's drop the bombs. Oops, I hope it wasn't London. The British came up with this in mid-1943. The Americans, in late 1943, we put them on about 50 B-24 and P-38 planes as Pathfinder planes.
cues.zh: 我们基本上是把雷达对准地面。云层和雨里都能看到目标。我们能看见主要地面特征的轮廓，并做地图叠加层：对，这里是汉堡，这里是河流，这里是海岸，这里应该是目标位置。投弹吧。哎呀，希望那不是伦敦。英国人在1943年中期搞出了这个。美国人到1943年末，把它装在大约50架B-24和P-38上，作为领航机。

cues.en: Regardless of the weather, by 1944 and 1945, our bombers would take off whether it was 100% cloud cover or not, and we'd bomb through overcast following the Pathfinder planes. Now, given all this, oh, and by the way, just to make this even more interesting, once we had this air-to-ground radar, the Germans noticed we had air-to-ground radar because we would turn it on way before the target to kind of test it out.
cues.zh: 不管天气如何，到1944和1945年，我们的轰炸机无论是否100%云层覆盖都会起飞，并跟随领航机穿过阴云轰炸。现在，考虑到这一切——哦，顺便说一句，让事情更有趣的是，一旦我们有了这种空对地雷达，德国人就注意到我们有空对地雷达，因为我们会在到达目标前很远就打开它来测试。

cues.en: Oops, they invented a radar receiver that would actually be able to track our planes because it was broadcasting a radar signal. We were a big beacon in the sky. So we were pathfinding our bombers. They invented a device called Naxos to track our air-to-ground radar. Catamouse game that went on all through in the war. Now, just a math challenge. For every hundred bombers on a mission, four to 20%.
cues.zh: 哎呀，他们发明了一种雷达接收机，实际上能追踪我们的飞机，因为它正在广播雷达信号。我们成了天空中的大信标。所以我们在为轰炸机领航时，他们发明了一种叫Naxos的装置来追踪我们的空对地雷达。猫鼠游戏贯穿整场战争。现在，只算一道数学题。每次任务每100架轰炸机，4%到20%……

cues.en: wouldn't return. Every 100 bombers, 4 to 20 percent wouldn't return. You had to fly 25 missions to go home. Kind of like the odds of a start-up in Silicon Valley. But the consequences were more profound. The Germans' goal was to make this prohibitively expensive in both material, which we could afford, but in air crews, which no military could afford. They wanted a turn
cues.zh: 不会返航。每100架轰炸机，有4%到20%不会返航。你得飞满25次任务才能回家。有点像硅谷创业公司的存活概率。但后果更深远。德国人的目标是让代价高到无法承受：物资我们承受得起，但机组人员任何军队都承受不起。他们想把

cues.en: these bombing missions into loss rates exceeding 20% for the Allies. And our goal was to drop those loss rates. This was a strategic issue for the entire Allied Air Command. What to do? And that's our second story. The second story is the electronic shield, electronic warfare. By 1942, the Allies realized that the German air defense system
cues.zh: 这些轰炸任务变成盟军损失率超过20%的局面。而我们的目标是降低这些损失率。这是整个盟军空军司令部的战略问题。怎么办？这就是我们的第二个故事。第二个故事是电子盾牌，电子战。到1942年，盟军意识到德国防空系统

cues.en: was going to take an enormous toll. And they needed to understand everything they didn't know. We didn't even know what radars the Germans had. We didn't know how effective. We didn't know how they were controlling anti-aircraft or fighters. So we needed to find out all this stuff, and then we needed to shut it down. So in 1942 and 43, we set up one of the most secret labs in the United States called the Harvard Radio Research Lab.
cues.zh: 会造成巨大损失。他们需要了解自己不知道的一切。我们甚至不知道德国人有哪些雷达。不知道它们有多有效。不知道他们如何控制防空炮或战斗机。所以我们需要查明所有这些，然后关掉它们。于是在1942和43年，我们建立了美国最机密的实验室之一，叫哈佛无线电研究实验室。

cues.en: focused on signals intelligence and electronic warfare. And its goal was to reduce allied losses to fighters in black. Number one, find and understand the German air defense system. There was no Google at the time. We could not Google German air defense system and get a list of all the radar. It didn't exist. Even more so, the techniques for electronics and signals intelligence didn't exist.
cues.zh: 专注于信号情报和电子战。其目标是减少盟军夜间遭战斗机造成的损失。第一，找到并理解德国防空系统。当时没有Google。我们没法谷歌德国防空系统，拿到所有雷达的清单。它不存在。更甚者，电子和信号情报的技术也不存在。

cues.en: And once we thought we'd understand it, then we needed to figure out how to shut it down. We wanted to understand the radar order of battle, that is, what radars came on when. And then we needed to build mechanical and electronic devices to shut down the Germans' ability to target and aim their weapons. This was a top secret 800-person lab. For those of you who have heard about the MIT radar lab,
cues.zh: 一旦我们以为搞懂了它，接下来就得想办法把它关掉。我们想弄清雷达战斗序列，也就是哪些雷达在什么时候开机。然后我们需要造机械和电子装置，破坏德国人瞄准和锁定武器的能力。这是一个绝密的800人实验室。你们中有人听说过MIT雷达实验室，

cues.en: This was even more secret than that. And in fact, every once in a while at MIT, when they were testing radar, stuff would work great, and then it would stop working. What they didn't realize is that on the other side of town, there were guys turning on jammers, and they were screwing with their radar on purpose. 40 years later, they get to tell each other these stories. Now, one of the problems with electronic intelligence, it's a line of sight problem. Radar traditionally goes in straight lines. So you've got to get close.
cues.zh: 这个实验室比那个还要机密。事实上，MIT时不时测试雷达时，设备会运行得很好，然后突然罢工。他们没意识到，在城镇另一头，有人正打开干扰机，故意捣乱他们的雷达。40年后，他们才能互相讲述这些故事。电子情报的一个问题是视距问题。雷达传统上沿直线传播。所以你必须靠近。

cues.en: if you want to understand what the enemy has. And so what we did was we essentially invented an electronics intelligence industry in about 12 months. These planes called ferrets, whose job they were to understand and find the German electronic air defense system. We stripped out B-24 bombers, took out all the bomb racks, took out all the bombs, took out even all the guns. And we filled it with racks of receivers and displays.
cues.zh: 如果你想弄清敌人有什么。于是我们做的，基本上是在大约12个月里发明了一个电子情报产业。这些飞机叫Ferrets，任务是了解并找到德国的电子防空系统。我们改装B-24轰炸机，拆掉所有炸弹架，卸下所有炸弹，甚至拆掉所有机枪。然后装满成架的接收机和显示器。

cues.en: Wire and strip recorders. Communications intercept equipment that could go from 50 megahertz to 3 gigahertz, and this is 1943. Flew these planes in and out of Germany, around the edges, inside, and basically built up the radar order of battle. First thing we decided to do was to shut down the Würzburg anti-aircraft radars and the Würzburg...
cues.zh: 钢丝录音机和条带记录仪。通信截获设备可覆盖50兆赫到3吉赫兹，而这是1943年。我们让这些飞机进出德国，绕着边缘、深入内部飞行，基本上建立起雷达战斗序列。我们决定做的第一件事，是瘫痪Würzburg防空雷达和Würzburg……

cues.en: ground control intercept radars that were directing the fighter planes. And to do that, instead of coming up with an electronic idea, the first thing we observed, which was observed in multiple countries at the same time, is that if you cut a strip of aluminum foil or a strip of any metallic object to half the wavelength of a radar set and throw it in front of the dish, the radar would reflect perfectly.
cues.zh: 以及引导战斗机的Würzburg地面控制拦截雷达。为了做到这一点，我们没有先提出电子方案；我们首先观察到——多个国家同时观察到——如果把一条铝箔或任何金属条剪到雷达波长的一半，再扔到天线碟前，雷达就会完美反射。

cues.en: from that half a wavelength strip of foil. Well, you couldn't stand in front of the German radars and thoroughd foil, but you could if you had a fleet of airplanes. And so the goal was to cut aluminum foil to half the Würzburg frequency, and I'll let you, as an exercise for the class, figure out how long the foil was. Frequency of the Würzburg is about 500 megahertz, so do the math. You could quickly figure it out. And each plane...
cues.zh: 也就是从那条半波长铝箔上反射回来。你不可能站在德国雷达前撒铝箔，但如果有飞机编队就可以。所以目标是按Würzburg频率对应的半波长来剪铝箔，我把算铝箔长度留给课堂练习。Würzburg频率约500兆赫，算算看。你们很快就能算出来。而每架飞机……

cues.en: threw out 46,000 packets of chaff on its first bombing mission by hand. 15,000 feet, they opened the door, and there was a guy, how'd you like to have the job? Oh yeah, you, stand by the door. And by the way, when the flack and fighter planes are coming, throw out the chaff. 46,000 packets, each packet had 2,000 strips. Now this would maybe be effective if it was one plane.
cues.zh: 在第一次轰炸任务中，纯靠人工扔出了 46,000 包箔条干扰丝。在一万五千英尺高空，舱门一开，有个人站在那——你想干这活吗？“对，就是你，站门边去。顺便说一句，高炮和敌机过来的时候，赶紧把箔条扔出去。”46,000 包，每包有 2,000 根。如果只有一架飞机，可能也就这点用了。

cues.en: But we were by then doing thousand plane missions. Now imagine a bomber stream dumping out a stream of aluminum foil across a city for the first time over Germany called Hamburg, July 1943. The raid on Hamburg was the first use of CHAF World War II. It completely shut down the German air defense system in and around Hamburg.
cues.zh: 但我们那时执行的已经是千机大轰炸了。想象一下，一支轰炸机编队在一座城市上空倾泻下一道铝箔长河——那是 1943 年 7 月，德国汉堡上空。突袭汉堡是二战中首次使用箔条。它彻底瘫痪了汉堡及其周边的德军防空系统。

cues.en: And for those who don't know the results, the British and then the Americans firebombed the city into the ground, completely destroyed Hamburg. Another interesting fact, used three quarters of all the aluminum foil in the US in World War II. And so there were all these aluminum foil drives, and people thought, how can they make airplanes out of aluminum foil? I can understand aluminum. This is where the aluminum foil was going. Because by the end of the war, every bomber stream.
cues.zh: 如果不了解结果的话，当时英军接着美军用燃烧弹将整座城市夷为平地，彻底摧毁了汉堡。另一个有趣的事实是，二战中全美四分之三的铝箔都用在了这上面。当时到处都在开展铝箔回收募捐，大家都在想，铝箔怎么可能造飞机？铝我能理解，但这铝箔都去哪儿了？其实全用在这儿了。因为到了战争末期，每支轰炸机编队……

cues.en: was dumping chaff on every mission. Now, that was kind of nice. It was mechanical, great. But the Harvard Radio Research Lab was really focused on electronic warfare. And so they systematically built devices to shut down each part of the German air defense system. If you remember the early warning radars, the Wasserman, Mammoth, and the Freya, we put jammers on every one of our airplanes. Something called the mandrel.
cues.zh: ……在每次任务中都会狂撒箔条。这招确实管用，纯机械手段，很棒。但哈佛无线电研究实验室真正专注的是电子战。于是他们系统化地研制设备，去瘫痪德军防空系统的各个环节。如果你还记得 Wasserman、Mammut 和 Freya 这些早期预警雷达，我们在每架飞机上都装了干扰机，一种叫做 Mandrel 的设备。

cues.en: The DINA, first on the escort fighters, then on bombers. Ridiculously small power output at the time. 12 watts, you gotta be kidding. But remember, you're flying in formation with a thousand other planes with their jammers on. Then we decided to shut down the Wurzburgs, which also controlled the flak and fighter ground control. The carpet jammers went on every one of our bombers just for scale. We built 20...
cues.zh: 还有 DINA，先装在护航战斗机上，接着装在轰炸机上。当时它的输出功率小得离谱，12 瓦，开什么玩笑？但别忘了，你是和一千架开着干扰机的飞机编队飞行的。随后我们决定干掉 Würzburg 雷达，它负责控制高炮和战斗机的地面引导。我们的每架轰炸机上都装了 Carpet 干扰机，仅从数量规模来看，我们造了 20……

cues.en: 4,000 of these, 24,000 jammers, just to jam the Würzburgs. There were entire factories in the US making nothing but the carpet jammer. And the British also had another problem, because remember they were bombing at night, and the German fighter planes had the night fighter radar, and so they had their own jammers. The airborne grocer and airborne cigar, which actually targeted the German ground control intercept radars,
cues.zh: ……4,000 台，两万四千台干扰机，仅仅为了干扰 Würzburg 雷达。当时美国有整座整座的工厂，专门生产 Carpet 干扰机。而英国人还有另一个难题，别忘了他们是在夜间轰炸，德军战机装有夜战雷达，所以英国人也搞了自己的干扰机：Airborne Grocer 和 Airborne Cigar，它们主要针对德军的地面引导拦截雷达。

cues.en: And sometimes they'd play speeches of Hitler to the German operators. And sometimes they'd try to spoof the German operators to confuse them in sending directions to the fighters to go the wrong place. This was on all British bombers. And the British actually came up with even something more sophisticated, a tail warning system that went on the back of every one of their bombers. And when the bombers were being illuminated by a German night fighter,
cues.zh: 有时他们会对着德军话务员播放希特勒的演讲；有时他们会伪造指令欺骗德军话务员，让他们把战斗机引导到错误的方向去。英国所有的轰炸机都装了这个。而且英国人还搞出了一套更精密的装置：安装在每架轰炸机尾部的机尾告警系统。当轰炸机被德军夜间战斗机雷达照射时，

cues.en: it would light up and say, hey, there's a night fighter who has its radar turned on and locked onto you. And that worked for about a week until one of those bombers crashed and the Germans saw it and they said, oh, we could build a device to actually look for that tail warning system. And so then one of the German fighters crashed and the British found that out and then they took out all the tail warning systems. Again, cat and mouse game for electronic warfare that still goes on today. By the end of World War II,
cues.zh: 它就会报警提示：“注意，有架夜战飞机开着雷达锁定你了。”这套系统管用了一个星期左右，直到有一架轰炸机坠毁，德国人发现了它，便说：“哦，我们可以专门造个设备去搜寻这个机尾告警系统的信号。”接着德军一架战机坠毁，英国人发现了这件事，于是把所有机尾告警系统全都拆掉了。这就是电子战中的猫鼠游戏，直到今天依然在继续。到了二战末期，

cues.en: over Europe, a bomber stream no longer consisted of planes with bombs. Sure, that was the mission, and in the core of a bomber stream, that's what you had, but by the end of the war, that bomber stream was surrounded by planes dumping chaff, by electronics intelligence planes looking for new radar signals, for fighter planes patrolling along with the bomber stream. The war changed dramatically, and we won.
cues.zh: 在欧洲上空，一支轰炸机编队里可不仅全是挂着炸弹的飞机。当然，轰炸是核心任务，编队中央也确实是轰炸机，但到了战末，这支轰炸机编队周围环绕着倾倒箔条的飞机、搜寻新雷达信号的电子侦察机，以及一路伴随巡逻的战斗机。战争形态发生了翻天覆地的变化，而我们赢了。

cues.en: They air war over Europe. But the interesting question, and 30 minutes into this presentation, is what the heck does this have to do with Silicon Valley? It's a great story. It's a lot of fun. But what on earth does this have to do with the valley? The question is, who ran this lab and became the father of electronic warfare for the next 50 years? Well, remember, the Harvard Radio Research, separate from MIT's lab,
cues.zh: 他们在欧洲上空进行空战。但有意思的问题是，这场演讲进行到30分钟时，这跟硅谷到底有什么关系？这是个精彩的故事。也很有趣。但这跟硅谷究竟有什么关系？问题是，谁运营了这个实验室，并成为未来50年的电子战之父？记住，Harvard Radio Research，与MIT的实验室是分开的，

cues.en: Ran all electronic warfare, 800 people. Director was Fred Terman of Stanford. Now, for those of you who don't know Fred Terman, he's known as one of the early fathers of Silicon Valley. And if you know anything about him, he was a Stanford professor of engineering in 1926, whose, I guess, public claim to fame was he encouraged his students, William Hewlett and David Packard, to start a company. And he's kind of known as kindly Professor Terman.
cues.zh: 管理所有电子战，800人。主任是斯坦福的 Fred Terman。现在，对不了解 Fred Terman 的人来说，他被认为是硅谷早期之父之一。如果你对他有所了解，他是1926年斯坦福的工程学教授；我猜他公众成名的原因，是他鼓励学生 William Hewlett 和 David Packard 创办公司。他大概被称为和蔼的 Terman 教授。

cues.en: He was dean of engineering in 1946, provost in 1955. And this is where things become fun. I'm going to talk about spook entrepreneurship. Now, just to give you some context, during World War II, the military changed dramatically and forever its relationships with universities in the United States. Pre-World War II,
cues.zh: 他1946年任工程学院院长，1955年任教务长。这时事情就变得有趣了。我要讲的是间谍创业。先给点背景：二战期间，美国军方与大学的关系发生了巨大且永久的改变。二战前，

cues.en: Military R&D were done in military labs. But in World War II, Vannevar Bush had an insight that said, let's put professors and universities to work in place. Let's enlist universities directly in the war effort. And we're going to fund the universities directly. So $450 million in 1945 dollars. Big bucks.
cues.zh: 军事研发都在军事实验室进行。但二战中，Vannevar Bush 有个洞见：让教授和大学就地投入工作。让大学直接参与战争努力。而且我们要直接资助大学。按1945年美元计，4.5亿美元。一大笔钱。

cues.en: MIT, 117 million, Caltech got 83, Harvard and Columbia got 30, forever changed their trajectory in technology. And oh, by the way, Stanford University got 50 grand. That's why Terman went east. That's why when they called him to run the Harvard Radio Research Lab, he knew they had no respect for Stanford as a technology university and had to go to Harvard to run this lab. But when he came back, he said,
cues.zh: MIT 1.17亿，Caltech 8300万，Harvard 和 Columbia 3000万，永远改变了它们在技术领域的发展轨迹。哦，顺便说，斯坦福大学只拿到5万美元。这就是 Terman 为什么去东部。这就是为什么当他们叫他去管理 Harvard Radio Research Lab 时，他知道他们不把斯坦福当技术大学看，他必须去哈佛管理这个实验室。但他回来后说，

cues.en: We're never getting screwed again. Terman with his war experience decided to build Stanford into a center of excellence on microwaves and electronics, and he was the guy to do it. The Harvard Radio Research Lab was the pinnacle in the United States of every advanced microwave transmitter and receiver you could think of. And what he does is he recruits 11 former members of the Radio Research Lab and says,
cues.zh: 我们绝不再被坑了。Terman 凭借战争经验，决定把斯坦福建成微波和电子学的卓越中心，而他正是做这件事的人。Harvard Radio Research Lab 是美国你能想到的各种先进微波发射机和接收机的巅峰。他做的是招募11名前 Radio Research Lab 成员，并说，

cues.en: You know, we really don't have a lab, but congratulations, you're all now Stanford faculty. And they went, oh, great, thanks. They joined Stanford, and they set up their own lab, the electronics research lab, for basic and unclassified research. And they get the Office of Naval Research to give them their first contract to actually fund, in the post-war, Stanford research into microwaves. By 1950, Terman turns.
cues.zh: 你知道，我们其实没有实验室，但恭喜，你们现在都是斯坦福的教职了。他们说，哦，太好了，谢谢。他们加入斯坦福，并建立自己的实验室——Electronics Research Lab，做基础和非机密研究。他们让 Office of Naval Research 给了他们第一份合同，实际资助战后斯坦福的微波研究。到1950年，Terman 开始出手。

cues.en: Stanford's engineering department into the MIT of the West. Basically, by taking all the war, innovative R&D and microwaves, by moving it to Stanford, by taking the department heads and key staff. But in the early 1950s, the Korean War changes the game. Post World War II, those of you who know your history, we basically demobilized our troops, mothballed our bombers and our fighters, and said, we're going to enjoy
cues.zh: 把斯坦福的工程系变成西部的 MIT。基本上，就是把战时的创新研发和微波技术搬到斯坦福，把系主任和核心人员带过去。但 1950 年代初，朝鲜战争改变了局面。二战后——了解历史的人都知道——我们基本遣散了部队，封存了轰炸机和战斗机，说我们要享受

cues.en: Just the post-war benefits. 1949, the Soviets explode their first nuclear weapon. The Cold War, where the Korean War becomes hot. All of a sudden, the United States realizes that the world's changed again. And spook work comes to Stanford. The military approaches Terman and asks him to set up the Applied Electronics Lab.
cues.zh: 只享受战后红利。1949 年，苏联引爆第一枚核武器。冷战之中，朝鲜战争变成热战。突然之间，美国意识到世界又变了。于是情报工作来到斯坦福。军方找到 Terman，请他建立应用电子实验室。

cues.en: to do classified military programs and doubles the size of the electronics program at Stanford. They said, well, we'll keep this separate from the unclassified electronics research lab. But for the first time, it made Stanford University a full partner with the military in government R&D. Now, you have to remember, this wasn't some rogue operation. This was actually great for the country. The Cold War truly could have become hot at any time.
cues.zh: 做机密军事项目，并让斯坦福的电子项目规模翻倍。他们说，好吧，我们会把它和非机密电子研究实验室分开。但这第一次让斯坦福大学成为军方在政府研发中的正式合作伙伴。你得记住，这不是什么擅自行动。这对国家其实大有好处。冷战真的随时可能变成热战。

cues.en: We were facing an implacable enemy, ideologically different from us, who was publicly determined to wipe us from the face of the earth. Having faced that before in World War II, Terman decides to dedicate all of his and Stanford's resources to help the U.S. understand what's going on inside the Soviet Union. We really felt there was the possibility of a nuclear Pearl Harbor.
cues.zh: 我们面对的是一个势不两立的敌人，意识形态与我们不同，公开决心要把我们从地球上抹去。Terman 在二战中已经面对过这种敌人，所以他决定把自己和斯坦福的全部资源投入进去，帮助美国了解苏联内部的情况。我们真的觉得，有可能发生一场核珍珠港事件。

cues.en: And all the techniques and technologies Terman had learned in World War II, electronics intelligence, signal intelligence, become critical again. And Stanford becomes a center of excellence for the National Security Agency and Central Intelligence Agency, as well as the military branches, whose goal it was to understand what's going on inside this closed country. Because the Cold War becomes an electronic war.
cues.zh: Terman 在二战中学到的所有技术和技巧——电子情报、信号情报——再次变得至关重要。斯坦福成为国家安全局、中央情报局以及各军种的卓越中心，他们的目标就是了解这个封闭国家内部的情况。因为冷战变成了一场电子战。

cues.en: The Russian air defense system is modeled after the Germans, but now they added serviced air missiles. All their fighters have radar, IFF. Our job was to understand it and defeat it, if necessary, in times of war. To understand it, you needed electronic intelligence. The Soviets were building intermediate range ballistic missiles and then intercontinental ballistic missiles. The only way we could even figure out the performance of the missiles, their accuracy, their throw weight,
cues.zh: 俄罗斯防空系统仿照德国人的系统，但现在他们加上了地对空导弹。他们所有战斗机都装有雷达和 IFF。我们的任务是理解它，并在战时必要时击败它。要理解它，就需要电子情报。苏联人当时在造中程弹道导弹，后来又在造洲际弹道导弹。我们甚至能弄清导弹性能、精度、投掷重量，以及

cues.en: lunchtime, et cetera, was that the Soviets adopted something the Germans developed during World War II, is when you're testing missiles, you actually add a little radio transmitter to the missile and sensors on all the critical systems, and you downlink telemetry to the ground to measure it. We got really good at knowing how to read Soviet telemetry almost before they could interpret their telemetry.
cues.zh: 当量等等——唯一办法，就是苏联采用了德国人在二战中开发的一种做法：测试导弹时，在导弹上加一个小型无线电发射机，在所有关键系统上装传感器，把遥测数据下传到地面来测量。我们变得非常擅长读取苏联遥测数据，几乎比他们自己解读得还早。

cues.en: During the Cold War, this was one of our major activities in understanding the Soviet missile threat. And of course, all the public things you read about photo reconnaissance with the Corona program and follow-ons to find the silos and bombers. And then the Soviet naval threat. Soviets by the late 1950s were starting to build ballistic missile submarines. We needed to understand them and we needed to understand the Soviet nuclear production infrastructure. All this in a closed country. In World War II,
cues.zh: 冷战期间，这是我们了解苏联导弹威胁的主要手段之一。当然，大家公开读到的，大多是通过 Corona 计划及其后续项目的照相侦察来寻找发射井和轰炸机。接着是苏联的海军威胁。到 50 年代末，苏联开始建造弹道导弹潜艇。我们需要了解这些，也需要摸清苏联的核生产基础设施。而这一切都发生在一个封闭国家。在二战中，

cues.en: we could fly over Germany. In the Cold War, that was supposedly illegal. It was an act of war. So how do you find out what's going on in a closed society? Well, Stanford helps understand the electronic order of battle. And remember, the electronic order of battle is where are the radars, and how will we encounter them? Because in the mid-1950s, our only strategic weapon was a manned bomber, by then the B-52.
cues.zh: 我们可以飞越德国上空。但在冷战中，这按理是非法的，属于战争行为。那么，你怎么查明一个封闭社会里发生的事？Stanford 协助摸清了电子战斗序列。记住，电子战斗序列就是：雷达都在哪儿？我们会如何遭遇它们？因为在 50 年代中期，我们唯一的战略武器就是有人驾驶轰炸机，也就是后来的 B-52。

cues.en: So the Strategic Air Command needed to know, the CIA needed to know, we needed details of the radars, so the NSA and CIA could give those details to contractors to build jammers, just like we did in World War II, to allow our B-52s to jam their radars, their Soviet radars, in case of war, to attack the targets. Now, it's one thing to understand the periphery of the Soviet Union, but the interior was just unknown. Can we turn up the audio?
cues.zh: 所以战略空军司令部需要知道，CIA 需要知道，我们需要雷达的细节，好让 NSA 和 CIA 把这些细节交给承包商制造干扰机，就像我们在二战中做的那样，以便让我们的 B-52 在战时干扰他们的雷达，苏联的雷达，进而打击目标。搞清苏联周边是一回事，但其内部完全是一无所知。能把音量调大一点吗？

cues.en: You know, if you remember what B-52 was like, it was kind of a four-engine plane, but its only payload were nuclear weapons. And the goal was to get under the Soviet radar, reach their target. Turn it up, please.
cues.zh: 如果你还记得 B-52 是什么样，它算是一种四发飞机，但它唯一的载荷就是核武器。它的目标是钻过苏联的雷达网，抵达目标。请把声音调大点。

cues.en: So you might remember this scene from Dr. Strangelove. But the serious thing was the B-52s were at this time on airborne alert. Their goal was to penetrate the Soviet Union. And if they hadn't had the second largest payload next to nuclear weapons, they're on board jammers. They wouldn't even get past the periphery.
cues.zh: 你们可能记得《奇爱博士》（Dr. Strangelove）里的这一幕。但严峻的现实是，当时的 B-52 处于空中警戒状态。它们的目标是突入苏联境内。而要不是它们携带了仅次于核武器的第二大载荷——机载干扰机——它们甚至连边境都穿不过去。

cues.en: but the plane was loaded with tens of thousands of pounds of jamming equipment. So problem one was to understand the Soviet radar order of battle. Our solution was to build a fleet of electronic intelligence planes that flew around the periphery of the Soviet block. This was a joint NSA CIA Air Force program and measured the Soviet air defense system and surprised the heck out of us. The Soviet low altitude coverage was good.
cues.zh: 但飞机上装载了数万磅的干扰设备。所以第一个问题是搞清苏联的雷达战斗序列。我们的解决方案是组建一支电子情报飞机机队，绕着苏联阵营的外围飞行。这是 NSA、CIA 和空军的联合项目，探测了苏联的防空系统，结果让我们大吃一惊：苏联的低空雷达覆盖非常好。

cues.en: So B-52s, which had initially been designed to go in at 30,000 feet and higher, actually changed their strategic operating plan by the 60s to go in at 200 feet, which made for a lot of hemorrhoids on B-52 pilots. Now, if you remember, for electronic intelligence, World War II, we had a line of sight problem. You got to get close. And more importantly, you got to get those radars turned on.
cues.zh: 因此，最初设计在 3 万英尺甚至更高空突防的 B-52，到了 60 年代实际上改变了战略作战计划，改在 200 英尺低空突防，这可把 B-52 飞行员颠出了不少痔疮。如果你还记得二战时的电子情报，我们面临视距限制的问题。你必须靠得足够近。更重要的是，你得想办法让那些雷达开机。

cues.en: Well, during the Cold War, we flew a lot of planes around the periphery of the Soviet Union to do that. And unfortunately, we lost 23 of them. This was a hot Cold War. Column on the left is the date. The victim is the type of plane, what service. And the stuff on the green on the right actually looks a little bizarre because it talks about the aircraft and the pilot and the weapon because this is a chart from the Soviet Union of who shot down what American electronic intelligence planes.
cues.zh: 嗯，冷战期间，为了做到这一点，我们沿着苏联外围飞了很多飞机。不幸的是，我们损失了 23 架。这是一场热冷战。左边一列是日期。受害者一栏是飞机类型、所属军种。右边绿色区域的内容其实看起来有点奇怪，因为它讲的是飞机、飞行员和武器，因为这是苏联的一张图表，记录谁击落了哪架美国电子情报飞机。

cues.en: We lost over 200 airmen in a hot war, in the Cold War, that no one ever heard about. But our goal was to try to understand what the order of battle looked like. So we decided that there might be a better way to get electronic intelligence. Now, how many of you have heard of the U-2? Almost everybody thinks of the U-2 as a photo reconnaissance plane. Its job is to fly across the Soviet Union and take photos of
cues.zh: 在一场没人听说过的热战中，在冷战中，我们损失了 200 多名空军人员。但我们的目标是弄清作战序列是什么样。所以我们认为，也许有更好的方式获取电子情报。现在，你们有多少人听说过 U-2？几乎所有人都把 U-2 当成照相侦察机。它的任务是飞越苏联，拍摄

cues.en: missile sites, defensive systems, et cetera. And yes, it did that. But it had another package where they unplugged the cameras and rolled in something else. U2 is a signal intelligence platform, courtesy of Stanford and Silicon Valley. 1956, System 4, designed by Stanford Electronics Lab and built by Ramo Woolwich, could cover 150 to 440 gigahertz. 1956.
cues.zh: 导弹基地、防御系统等等。没错，它确实这么做了。但它还有另一个载荷：他们拔掉相机，装入别的东西。U2 是一个信号情报平台，这要归功于 Stanford 和硅谷。1956 年的 System 4 由 Stanford Electronics Lab 设计、Ramo Woolwich 制造，可覆盖 150 到 440 吉赫兹。1956 年。

cues.en: communications and electronics intelligence package flying along and then inside the Soviet Union from day one had an electronic intelligence receiver even on the planes that carried photo equipment and then started looking for telemetry. First signal intelligence intercepts of missiles in flight came from the U2 and then it had onboard jammers and all Silicon Valley companies started participating in programs like these.
cues.zh: 通信与电子情报载荷一路飞行，然后进入苏联；从第一天起，即使是在携带照相设备的飞机上，也装有电子情报接收机，随后开始搜寻遥测信号。对飞行中导弹的首次信号情报截获来自 U2；后来它又装了机载干扰器，所有硅谷公司都开始参与这类项目。

cues.en: designed at Stanford, built by Valley companies. What was interesting is Stanford joins the black world the days Terman becomes provost. If you remember, the electronics research lab did basic and unclassified research. The applied electronics lab was the classified side. They merged in 1955 when Terman became provost and said, I have enough political cover to do this.
cues.zh: 在 Stanford 设计，由硅谷公司制造。有意思的是，就在 Terman 当上教务长时，Stanford 加入了机密世界。如果你还记得，电子研究实验室做基础和非机密研究。应用电子实验室是机密那一侧。1955 年 Terman 成为教务长时，它们合并了，他说：我有足够的政治掩护来做这件事。

cues.en: Stanford is now, in its engineering department, basically advanced R&D for NSA, CIA throughout the Cold War. Now, that's kind of interesting, but what does this have to do with entrepreneurship? This is where the valley changed to something we could recognize today. It starts right here. In doing so, Terman believed he was fighting for our country, that he was going to do whatever was necessary
cues.zh: 在整个冷战期间，Stanford 的工程系基本上就是 NSA、CIA 的高级研发部门。这挺有意思，但这跟创业有什么关系？硅谷正是在这里变成了我们今天能认出的样子。一切就从这里开始。这样做时，Terman 相信他是在为我们的国家而战，他要做任何必要的事

cues.en: to make us the most innovative war fighting machine that we could be. So he changes the rules at a university. Here's what he did. This is the mid 1950s. Instead of encouraging his graduate students to start companies, excuse me, to get PhDs, he encourages them to leave and start companies.
cues.zh: 让我们成为最具创新性的作战机器。于是他改变了一所大学的规则。他是这么做的。这是 1950 年代中期。他没有鼓励研究生去创业——抱歉，说错了，是去读博士——而是鼓励他们离开学校去创业。

cues.en: He encourages professors to consult for companies. In fact, heredically, Terman and other professors take board seats outside of Stanford. And he made any IP transfer you saw, anything you wanted in his lab, take it. Here, sign this piece of paper. Boom, you're out. Licensing didn't take three years. It took three minutes at Stanford. Getting out in the real world was good for your academic career. This was heretical.
cues.zh: 他鼓励教授为公司做咨询。事实上，特曼和其他教授打破常规，在斯坦福之外担任董事。他让实验室里你想要的任何知识产权转让都直接拿走。来，签这张纸。砰，你就能拿走。许可不需要三年，在斯坦福三分钟就搞定。走向现实世界对你的学术生涯有好处。这是反传统的。

cues.en: No one was doing this. And more importantly, Terman had another observation. He said, I do not want to build production systems for the military. I want to do research. I want other people to start companies and have the military fund them. And these are the companies we'll consult for and sit on boards. And so the valley blossoms in the mid-1950s. It becomes Microwave Valley.
cues.zh: 没人这么做。更重要的是，特曼还有另一个观察。他说，我不想为军方建生产系统。我想做研究。我想让别人创办公司，让军方资助他们。而我们就是为这些公司做咨询、担任董事。于是这个谷在20世纪50年代中期繁荣起来，变成微波谷。

cues.en: And here's just an example of maybe five or 10 out of the hundreds of microwave companies that blossom to do military R&D work. First for components, and then we'll see later systems, starting with Varian after the war, Linton Industries, Huggins, Stewart, Watkins, Johnsons, MEC, et cetera. But things get even more interesting in the late 50s and the early 60s. And the CIA and NSA become incredibly creative.
cues.zh: 这里只是数百家涌现出来做军事研发的微波公司中的五到十个例子。先是做元器件，之后我们会看到系统，从战后的 Varian 开始，还有 Linton Industries、Huggins、Stewart、Watkins、Johnsons、MEC 等等。但到了50年代末和60年代初，事情变得更有意思。CIA 和 NSA 变得极具创意。

cues.en: And let me give you an example. In 1960, there was something called Project Melody. It was noticed in the mid-1950s when the CIA was flying high-altitude balloons across the Soviet Union. Don't you know that? So in the 1950s, we decided before the U-2, the way we were going to take pictures of the Soviet Union, we were going to build these 10-story balloons, fill them with helium, put giant cameras underneath them,
cues.zh: 让我举个例子。1960年有个叫 Project Melody 的项目。事情可以追溯到50年代中期，当时 CIA 正让高空气球飞越苏联。你不知道吧？所以50年代，在 U-2 之前，我们决定这样拍苏联：造十层楼高的气球，灌满氦气，下面挂巨型相机，

cues.en: pop them up into the jet stream and hope they come out at the other end of the Soviet Union. We launched hundreds of them, except they kept coming down in Soviet farms with these giant 600-pound cameras. Though we did get, we covered about 8% of the Soviet Union, politically it was pretty nasty because we launched about 400 of these balloons and only got 32 at the other end. And that meant, you know, there was about 380 popping up in Khrushchev's desk. Oh, another balloon. Wasn't very happy.
cues.zh: 把它们送入急流，希望它们从苏联另一端出来。我们发射了数百个，结果它们不断落在苏联农场上，还带着这些600磅重的巨型相机。我们确实有所收获，覆盖了约8%的苏联领土；但政治上很难看，因为我们发射了约400个气球，只有32个到达另一端。这意味着，你知道，大约380个会出现在赫鲁晓夫的办公桌上。“哦，又来一只气球。”他可不怎么高兴。

cues.en: But these were just camera balloons, but what we noticed was kind of interesting. We were kind of looking for the balloons near the periphery of the Soviet Union with our radar, and we noticed we were picking up a Soviet radar being received in our radar set. Turned out there was a piece of metal in the balloon that happened to be cut accidentally to the exact frequency of a Soviet height-finding radar that was trying to track these balloons, and that signal was bouncing off
cues.zh: 但这些只是相机气球，不过我们注意到的情况挺有意思。我们当时用雷达在苏联边缘附近寻找这些气球，结果发现我们的雷达设备收到了一个苏联雷达信号。原来气球里有一块金属，碰巧被切割成正好对应苏联测高雷达频率的尺寸，那部雷达正试图跟踪这些气球，而信号正从

cues.en: that piece of metal and being picked up in ours. And somebody said, huh, gee, that's an accident. I wonder if we could do that on purpose. And let's actually design something on purpose called the bistatic intercept receiver. That is, you could have an uncooperative transmitter not even knowing that it was transmitting, being bounced off of something and picked up by another receiver. Just as a piece of irony, the Germans actually invented this in World War II as an active system.
cues.zh: 那块金属上反射，并被我们的设备接收到。有人就说，嘿，天哪，这是偶然。不知道能不能故意这么做。于是我们干脆故意设计一个叫双基地截获接收机的东西。也就是说，可以让一个非合作发射机甚至在不知情的情况下发射，信号经某物体反射，被另一台接收机收到。讽刺的是，德国人其实在二战时就把它作为有源系统发明了。

So they said, hey, this bistatic radar stuff, pretty good. But instead of you waiting for the Soviets to launch an ICBM, doesn't the moon go over the Soviet Union? Why, yes, it does. Well,
cues.zh: 升级成了叫 Tall King 的东西。我们需要知道它们在哪里，有多少。B-52 轰炸机最终会需要这些信息，但中情局急需在决定 A-12 能否飞越苏联之前搞清楚这一点。所以他们说，嘿，这双基地雷达的东西挺不错。但与其等苏联发射洲际弹道导弹，月亮不是也会经过苏联上空吗？对，确实会。那么，

cues.en: Aren't Soviet radar signals going out into space? Why, yes, they are. Couldn't we, like, intercept those signals when the moon and the Soviet Union kind of line up in the right way? Why, yes, we could. So let's point our dishes at the moon and use the moon as a bi-static reflector and listen for the Tolkien signals. And as the earth and the moon rotated about once a month, everything would line up. The problem is you needed really big dishes. Big dishes. Big.
cues.zh: 苏联雷达信号不是会射向太空吗？对，确实会。那当月球和苏联以合适方式排成一线时，我们难道不能截获那些信号吗？对，我们可以。所以，把我们的天线对准月球，把月球当作双基地反射器，监听 Tall King 信号。随着地球和月球转动，大约每月会有一次对齐。问题是你需要非常大的天线。大天线。大。

cues.en: dishes. So radio dishes in 1958, 1960 get funded. All of a sudden, the United States was the most interested country in the world in radio astronomy. Every university, you want a dish? Absolutely. But by the way, we need to borrow it for about an hour, every 28 days, 302. But don't worry, we won't take up much time. And so we attached Eland receivers. First, we tried it at Bell Labs. He used the match filter techniques to develop the Terman's lab.
cues.zh: 天线。于是射电望远镜天线在1958、1960年获得了资助。突然间，美国成了全世界对射电天文学最感兴趣的国家。每所大学都想要一口天线？当然想。但顺便说一下，我们每隔28天要借用它大约一小时，302。别担心，不会占用太多时间。于是我们装上了Elint接收机。我们先在贝尔实验室试过，他用匹配滤波技术开发了特曼实验室。

Now, we kept going higher and higher, and getting Elon to, you know, we're using the moon now, we were using U2s. The ultimate altitude was space. Some of the first satellites were actually electronic intelligence. No more overflights. So let's collect radar emissions.
cues.zh: 在Sugar Grove建了一座可转向天线，然后我们出资建了斯坦福的天线。凡是去"the dish"徒步的人——有人在那里徒步过吗？谢谢CIA。后来我们越飞越高，还拉上了埃隆，你知道的，我们现在用上了月球，之前用U2侦察机。终极高度是太空。最早的一批卫星其实是电子情报卫星。不再需要越境飞越了。我们来收集雷达辐射信号。

cues.en: From Soviet air defense radars, we launched this first satellite in 1960. If you remember, we got into space only in 1958. That's how strategically important Project Grab was. Built by the NRO, then used by the Strategic Air Command to figure out the electronic order of battle and then given to the National Reconnaissance Office. And not to be outdone, the Navy goes, well, wait a minute. Biggest problem in World War II was figuring out where the enemy's fleet are. So let's...
cues.zh: 卫星于1960年发射，用来收集苏联防空雷达的信号。还记得吗，我们1958年才进入太空。可见“Grab”计划在战略上有多重要。它由国家侦察办公室（NRO）的前身建造，之后被战略空军司令部用来弄清电子作战序列，后来又交给了国家侦察办公室。海军也不甘示弱，说：等等，二战中最大的难题就是搞清敌方舰队的位置。那我们……

cues.en: put Elent in space. Naval ships are notorious emitters. They have radios and radars and all kinds of stuff going on, but the problem is you can never find fleets in the middle of the ocean. Now they can no longer hide. We'll collect radio and radar emissions from Soviet Naval vessels, and this time we'll put up clusters of satellites to triangulate and direction find. And so, Elent gets to the ultimate heights. The valley becomes a microwave valley.
cues.zh: 把Elint搬上太空。海军舰艇是出了名的信号发射源，它们有无线电、雷达，各种设备都在运作，但问题是在茫茫大海中你永远找不到舰队。现在它们再也无法躲藏了。我们要收集苏联海军舰艇的无线电和雷达辐射信号，这次我们会发射卫星集群，用来三角定位和测向。就这样，Elint达到了终极高度。谷地变成了微波谷。

cues.en: Not only are those component manufacturers, but now we're also systems manufacturers. Probably the most famous precursor to most spook companies that were systems players other than Lockheed, Sylvania's Electronic Defense Laboratory, Bill Perry, who became Secretary of Defense, started here, founded ESL, GE's Microwave Lab, Grainger Associates, and ESL. All examples of alumni, Argo systems, et cetera.
cues.zh: 这里不仅是元器件制造商的聚集地，如今还成了系统制造商的聚集地。在洛克希德之外，可能是大多数间谍公司中最著名的系统类前辈——Sylvania的电子防御实验室，后来成为国防部长的比尔·佩里就是从这里起步的，他创立了ESL；还有GE的微波实验室、Grainger Associates和ESL，Argo Systems等等，都是这批“校友”的例子。

cues.en: What's interesting is to think about what Terman did for entrepreneurship. Basically, if we have the entire semester, I'll go through the entire chart. But basically, the motivation for Terman and Silicon Valley in the 1950s and the 1960s was the Cold War crisis, not profit. Big idea. Country faced a life and death struggle.
cues.zh: 有意思的是去思考特曼对创业精神做了什么。 basically，如果有整整一个学期的时间，我可以把整张图谱都讲一遍。但简单来说，1950和1960年代特曼与硅谷的动机是冷战危机，而不是利润。这是个重要的观点。当时国家面临生死存亡的斗争。

cues.en: and the motivation for entrepreneurship here was crisis, and it was funding entrepreneurs with military finance. By the way, why it's called Silicon Valley, on the other side of town, the head of radar bombing training, remember that air-to-ground radar I showed you? The head of training for the US Air Force decides to start a company. This guy was the director of Naval Anti-Submarine Warfare Ops at Columbia.
cues.zh: 这里创业的动机是危机，是用军方资金资助创业者。顺便说，为什么叫硅谷——在城的另一头，雷达轰炸训练负责人，记得我给你看过的空对地雷达吗？美国空军训练负责人决定创办公司。这家伙曾是哥伦比亚大学海军反潜作战行动主管。

cues.en: had a radar bombing training for the Air Force, Deputy Director of all of weapons R&D in the middle of the Cold War. He knew every secret that we had, but didn't like the job. Because he had left, his other company was looking for what to do. He called up Terman. He said, yeah, I grew up in this area. I'm thinking of coming back and doing what I did in my last company, because he was the co-inventor of the transistor. William Shockley, the other father of Silicon Valley, had a military background, probably his deepest term.
cues.zh: 他为空军做雷达轰炸训练，冷战中期所有武器研发的副主任。他知道我们所有的秘密，但不喜欢那份工作。他离开后，他原来的公司也在找方向。他打电话给 Terman。他说，是啊，我在这片地区长大。我想回来，做我上一家公司做过的事，因为他是晶体管的共同发明人。William Shockley，硅谷的另一位父亲，有军方背景，这大概是他最深的渊源。

cues.en: Terman Excuse me Shockley as you might know known as the world's best researcher awesome talent spotter and probably the worst manager except for maybe some of your bosses, but Unintended consequence he starts Shockley semiconductor Trader receipt leave Shockley a couple years later found Fairchild noise and more found leave Fairchild to fund Intel in the first 20 years after Shockley 65 other chip companies start
cues.zh: Terman——抱歉，是 Shockley——你可能知道，他被认为是世界上最好的研究者、极佳的识人者，也可能是最差的经理，也许仅次于你们某些老板。但意外后果是，他创办了 Shockley Semiconductor。几年后，叛徒八人组离开 Shockley，创办 Fairchild Semiconductor；摩尔和诺伊斯离开 Fairchild，创办 Intel。Shockley 之后的头20年里，又有65家芯片公司成立。

cues.en: from him. His eugenics belief ends his career in 1963. You could see Shockley kind of on the left. Let me zoom out for, what, 23 years or 20 years of semiconductors. That's him. Sixty-five other companies came because this one guy who worked on air-to-ground radar in World War II, who happened to invent the transistor, started in Silicon Valley. His legacy, it's Silicon Valley. If I can, five more minutes, last story.
cues.zh: 都源自他。他的优生学信仰在1963年终结了他的职业生涯。你能看到 Shockley 差不多在左边。让我拉远看——大概23年，或者20年的半导体历史。那就是他。另外65家公司出现，是因为这个人在二战中研究空对地雷达，又碰巧发明了晶体管，并在硅谷创业。他的遗产，就是硅谷。如果可以，再给我五分钟，讲最后一个故事。

cues.en: why we don't all work for the government, the rise of private capital. If you remember, what drove Terman was crisis and military finance. The valley, as we know it today, is profit and venture finance. What happened? This was gonna be microwave valley. What changed? Well, in the mid-1950s,
cues.zh: 为什么我们不是都在为政府工作：私人资本的崛起。如果你还记得，驱动 Terman 的是危机和军方资金。我们今天所知的这个谷，是利润与风险投资。发生了什么？这里本来会成为微波谷。什么变了？嗯，在1950年代中期，

cues.en: The first valley companies go public, Varian, HP, Ampex. People start noticing that there's something interesting going on here. And it turns out that venture capital, as we know it, actually started as family money. In the early 1940s, J.H. Whitney wrote essentially his own family office a check for five million bucks and said, go invest. Lawrence Rockefeller did the same thing with a family office.
cues.zh: 硅谷第一批公司上市：Varian、HP、Ampex。人们开始注意到这里有些有趣的事情发生。结果，我们今天所知的风险投资，其实起源于家族资金。1940年代初，J.H. Whitney 基本上是给自己家族办公室开了张500万美元的支票，说：去投资吧。Lawrence Rockefeller 也用家族办公室做了同样的事。

cues.en: So did Bessemer. But these were essentially East Coast focused companies, wide variety of industries. And on the East Coast, venture capital kind of also takes form in some experiments around Boston. American Research and Development, Georgia Rowe. Probably the first VC firm with the right structure, wrong model. Anybody know the company he funded? DEC, Digital Equipment Corporation, gave him 75 grand, I think he got 80% of the company.
cues.zh: Bessemer 也是如此。但这些本质上都是聚焦东海岸的公司，横跨各种行业。在东海岸，风险投资也以波士顿周边的一些实验形式出现。American Research and Development，Georges Doriot。大概第一家结构正确、模式错误的VC公司。有人知道他投了哪家公司吗？DEC，Digital Equipment Corporation，给了他7.5万美元，我想他拿了公司80%的股份。

cues.en: Oh, those were the days. He had the right idea, but the wrong model. He took his VC firm public and had a deal with the SEC. Some of the spin outs out of him were Boston Capital. Out here in Silicon Valley, a bunch of essentially angels who called themselves the group started in the 1950s. They did their first 10 deals, funded entire companies for 75 grand to 300 grand. Someone's still in business. Reed Dennis said,
cues.zh: 真是令人怀念的岁月。他的想法很对，但模式错了。他把自己的风投公司弄上市，还得跟 SEC 打交道。从他那里衍生出的机构包括 Boston Capital。而在硅谷这边，一群本质上是天使投资人、自称“组织”（The Group）的人在 1950 年代起步。他们做了最初的 10 笔交易，投一家完整的公司只要 7.5 万到 30 万美元。有的至今还在营业。Reed Dennis 曾说：

cues.en: The first 25 electronics companies required total capital of 300K each, and private individuals were on the basis of the early syndicates. In 1975, the entire VC industry raised $10 million. Well, for those of you in startups, repeat that. The entire VC industry raised $10 million. But in 1958, the world kind of changed. The Small Business Administration said, hey, we'll match you two for one. For every dollar you put in, we'll put in two.
cues.zh: 前 25 家电子公司每家只需要 30 万美元的总资金，而早期的投资辛迪加基本都是个人投资者。1975 年，整个风投行业只募集了 1000 万美元。搞创业的朋友们，请再听一遍：整个风投行业只募集了 1000 万美元。但在 1958 年，世界开始变了。小企业管理局（SBA）表示：“嘿，我们给你 1 比 2 配资。你每投 1 美元，我们就出 2 美元。”

cues.en: And so by 1968, 75% of VC funding was coming from the SBA. And in fact, corporations set up their own SBAs. Bank of America, Fireman's Fund, and private companies did so as well. But venture was still trying to figure out what the right model for investing is. Now just while all this is going on, here's some scale. These are normalized billions of dollars on the left.
cues.zh: 因此到了 1968 年，75% 的风投资金都来自 SBA。事实上，各大企业也设立了自己的 SBA。Bank of America、Fireman's Fund 以及私营企业都这么做了。但风投界仍在摸索什么是合适的投资模式。在这一切发生的同时，我们来看个规模对比。左边是折算后的十亿美元数据。

cues.en: Here's the defense R&D budget from 1953 to about 73. Here's California's take on that budget. Here's Silicon Valley's take on the military R&D budget. You can see that's kind of a small green percent of a percent of a percent. But let me scale venture capital. Can you see that? Let me zoom in for you. Can you see it now? Venture capital pre-1972.
cues.zh: 这是 1953 年到大约 1973 年的国防研发预算。这是加州从中分得的份额。这是硅谷从军工研发预算中拿到的份额。你可以看到，那只是一小抹绿色，微乎其微。但让我把风险投资也放进来对比一下。能看到吗？我给大家放大一下。现在看得到吗？1972 年之前的风险投资，

cues.en: was infinitesimal in Silicon Valley. Funding for companies was military finance, but things changed. Starting in the early 60s, a set of innovative entrepreneurs in finance decide that there's a business to start funding companies in Silicon Valley. And here are some of the early ones, some still in business, like Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia.
cues.zh: 在硅谷简直微不足道。当时公司的资金主要来自军方拨款，但情况发生了变化。从 60 年代初开始，金融界一批具有创新精神的创业者认定，在硅谷资助初创公司是一门好生意。这里列出了一些早期的机构，有些至今仍在营业，比如 Kleiner Perkins 和 Sequoia。

cues.en: And in 1978 and 1979, a watershed happens. Life changes completely and VCs explode because the government decides to make two simple changes. They slash capital gains. That is the amount of tax on stock profits from essentially 50% to 28%. VCs go, oh man, there's a ton of money to be made. And they tell pension funds, hey.
cues.zh: 到了 1978 和 1979 年，转折点出现了。局面彻底改变，风投行业迎来大爆发，因为政府做出了两项简单的调整。他们大幅削减了资本利得税——也就是股票收益税，基本上从 50% 砍到了 28%。风投们惊呼：“天呐，这里有大把的钱可赚。”接着他们对养老基金说：

cues.en: You want to invest in a VC fund? Sure. You could put up to 10% of your pension fund into VCs. The amount of money going into VCs jumps by a factor of 10. All of a sudden, Silicon Valley's second engine of entrepreneurship takes off by 1979. And what we're funding is now for profit. So in summary.
cues.zh: “想投资风投基金吗？没问题，你可以把最多 10% 的养老基金投进风投。”流入风投的资金瞬间激增了 10 倍。转眼间，到了 1979 年，硅谷的第二个创业引擎轰鸣启动。而我们投资的目标，现在完全是以营利为目的了。总结一下。

cues.en: Turman, Stanford, and the government is responsible for the entrepreneurial culture of Silicon Valley. The military primed the pump as a customer for key technologies. We've all heard the stories about the first semiconductors and Minimend guidance systems, government's interest in computers at NSA and Livermore. And of course, DARPA's interest in packet switching and the internet. But there's been very, very little technology cross-pollinization.
cues.zh: Turman、Stanford 和政府共同促成了硅谷的创业文化。军方作为关键技术的客户，起到了启动作用。我们都听过那些故事：最早的半导体和 Minimend 制导系统，以及政府通过 NSA 和 Livermore 对计算机产生的兴趣。当然，还有 DARPA 对分组交换和互联网的兴趣。但技术上的交叉融合非常非常少。

cues.en: Not none, but very little. The government has been a great customer. But it turns out that it's venture capital that turned the valley to volume corporate and consumer applications within an infinitesimal amount of dollars compared to what the military put into the valley. So a question I'll just leave you with, is there another crisis that will restart the valley cycle of innovation? Or will we continue to be profit driven? So something to think about and thank you for sitting through a long presentation.
cues.zh: 并非没有，但非常少。政府一直是很棒的客户。但事实证明，是风险投资让硅谷转向大规模的企业级和消费级应用，而相比军方投入硅谷的资金，风投用的钱少得微不足道。所以，我留给你们一个问题：还会有另一场危机重启硅谷的创新周期吗？还是我们会继续被利润驱动？值得思考一下。谢谢大家听完这场漫长的演讲。
